description:
Iranian media says several vessels, including oil tankers, have begun crossing the Strait of Hormuz following the signing of a memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran.

The reports are being seen in Tehran as a possible goodwill gesture ahead of Friday's in-person signing ceremony in Geneva.

However, US officials are warning that a full reopening of the strategic waterway could still take weeks, citing demining operations and ongoing security concerns.

The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important energy corridors, and any disruption there has major implications for global oil markets.

At the same time, differences remain over sanctions relief and the release of Iran's frozen assets. Tehran views these issues as central to the agreement, while Washington says any easing of sanctions will depend on Iran's compliance during future negotiations.

The deal has lowered tensions, but major questions remain over implementation and the future of US-Iran r
title: First Ships Cross Strait of Hormuz After US-Iran Deal

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
US President Donald Trump says a Memorandum of Understanding between the United States and Iran has been signed electronically, with an in-person signing ceremony expected to take place in Geneva on Friday.

Speaking ahead of the G7 summit in France, Trump said Vice President JD Vance would attend the ceremony and added that the Strait of Hormuz is already beginning to reopen to shipping traffic.

French President Emmanuel Macron welcomed the agreement, calling it an important step toward addressing concerns over Iran's nuclear programme and bringing greater stability to the Middle East.

France and the United Kingdom are now discussing an international maritime mission to help secure the Strait of Hormuz and reassure global shipping.

The agreement is expected to dominate discussions at the G7 summit, where leaders from several Middle Eastern countries, including Qatar, the UAE and Egypt, have also been invited.

title: Iran deal dominates G7 Summit as leaders welcome breakthrough.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
US President Donald Trump is presenting the agreement with Iran as a major diplomatic victory, saying it will reopen the Strait of Hormuz and pave the way for a broader settlement.

But Al Jazeera's senior political analyst Marwan Bishara says the deal raises difficult questions, including whether Washington is claiming credit for ending a crisis that it helped create.

Bishara argues that many of the objectives now being pursued were already addressed under the 2015 nuclear agreement, which Trump withdrew from during his first term.

He also warns that while both Washington and Tehran appear to need a deal, the road ahead will be complicated by deep mistrust, unresolved disputes and the possibility that regional actors, particularly Israel, could try to undermine the agreement.

The memorandum of understanding may have opened the door to diplomacy, but whether it can deliver a lasting peace in the Middle East remains uncertain.

description:
A large overnight Russian missile and drone barrage has killed at least 11 people across Ukraine, wounded 53 and knocked out power to 140,000 households. The attack ignited a major fire at the Dormition Cathedral within the UNESCO‑listed Kyiv‑Pechersk Lavra monastery – the spiritual heart of Ukrainian Orthodoxy. It also heavily damaged the Oleksandr Dovzhenko National Film Studios, destroying a collection of roughly 100,000 costumes.
Metropolitan Epiphanius I condemned the attack as “a crime against humanity”. In Kharkiv, a “double‑tap” strike killed five rescuers who were extinguishing an earlier fire. President Zelenskyy said Russia’s actions show its intention to continue the war, calling for a decisive G7 response and more air defence support. Asked by Al Jazeera for his response, he said solemnly: “We will see. We will see. Anyway, we all always respond.” His comments came after a phone call with US President Donald Trump on Sunday, where they discussed peace and a future meeting
title: Russian attacks in Ukraine kill 11, damage historic Kyiv cathedral

He described the MOU as a result of “Iranian steadfastness and resistance” against what he called two “devils” (the US and Israel). Iran gives no concessions in phase one except agreeing to discuss the nuclear file later and reopening the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian management. He explained that Iran imposed a two phase structure on the talks, despite US insistence on a single package. The first phase includes confidence building measures; the second phase will address a final deal. Dareini stressed that from Iran’s standpoint, the memorandum of understanding is a continuation of war – not an agreement, but a limited deal for a limited period. The UK government has won its appeal to uphold the designation of Palestine Action as a “terrorist” group. The activist group was banned last year after being accused of breaking into an airbase as part of its ongoing protests Israel's genocide in Gaza. Rights groups say more than 3,000 people have been arrested for publicly supporting the group, and more than 1,200 protesters have been charged with terrorism-related offences under the ban.
The Court of Appeal in London ruled that it had struck a balance between national interest and the rights of individuals. The judge said that while there were peaceful members of Palestine Action, there were also non‑peaceful members whose actions amounted to terrorism. The court upheld the government’s proscription of Palestine Action, which began in July 2024 following a series of high‑profile protests that caused damage at defence establishments.

US President Donald Trump announced what he described as a "peace deal" with Iran, while Tehran said the agreement also includes a ceasefire in Lebanon. The announcement came just hours after an Israeli air strike on Beirut’s southern suburb of Dahiyeh killed three people and wounded 16.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the military targeted Hezbollah sites in response to the group firing into northern Israel. US President Donald Trump condemned the attack.
The conflict in Lebanon has lasted four months, with nearly 3,800 people killed and nearly 12,000 wounded. Many Hezbollah fighters are still believed to be buried under rubble. There is cautious optimism and relief, but large-scale returns to homes have not yet taken place as people wait for further details.
The Israeli army still occupies dozens of villages in southern Lebanon, and Israeli officials have made clear they are not withdrawing as part of the deal.

A Jewish anti-Zionist activist disrupted an Israeli real estate event at a synagogue in west London, as protesters gathered outside to oppose the marketing of property linked to Israeli settlements.

Police dispersed demonstrators and made several arrests after the protest moved onto nearby roads and blocked traffic.

Some of the properties being advertised are believed to include land in occupied East Jerusalem and Gush Etzion in the occupied West Bank, territories that are considered occupied Palestinian land under international law.

More than 100 British MPs have signed a letter urging the government to ban such events, arguing that promoting property in illegal settlements is inconsistent with international law.

A recent report by Amnesty International says the expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has accelerated under the current Israeli government.

title: Protests Erupt at Israeli Real Estate Event in London Synagogue

Leaders of the G7 nations and invited guests from several other countries are gathering on the shores of Lake Geneva for one of the most consequential summits in recent years.

The meeting comes amid efforts to end the conflict involving Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

Leaders from Qatar, the UAE and Egypt have been invited to discuss the implications of the crisis for the Middle East, while concerns over the global economy and energy prices continue to grow.

The summit is also expected to focus on the wars in Gaza and Ukraine, international trade, tariffs and the rapid rise of artificial intelligence.

Analysts say divisions among allies and President Donald Trump's increasingly transactional approach to diplomacy could make this one of the most challenging G7 meetings in decades.
